title: Prediction, Validation, and Marketing Actions
objectives: Design a holdout that matches deployment and prevents leakage.
Compare ranking, calibration, and decision costs.
Assess coverage and missing future labels in an availability forecast.
Compare identical rankings with different probability losses and demand forecasts.
Construct prediction intervals and label sets; compare marginal coverage with segment and routing outcomes.
Evaluate grader coverage and asymmetric error costs against explicit reference judgments.
Separate anomaly detection, variable localization, event timing, and evidence for a diagnosis.
Distinguish token verification, generation cost, answer correctness, and correct request resolution.
Explain how training mixtures change feature attribution and evaluate outcomes by service context and checkpoint rule.
Evaluate omitted auxiliary bias separately from sampling variance.
Distinguish oracle group purity from held-out prediction and detect label use during preprocessing.
Compare reconstruction, component errors, feature interpretation, and decision outcomes.

slides.title: A Service-Capacity Decision
bullets: A team can review 100 customers each week.
Predictions use information available before that week.
The outcome and review benefit determine the useful metric.
slides.notes: A model selected on overall accuracy can fail to identify the cases that the team can help. The intervention value and the forecast are separate quantities.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Validation Reproduces Deployment
slides.caption: The deployment population determines the appropriate holdout.
slides.description: Random rows, whole-customer holdouts, and later-period holdouts test different forms of generalization.
slides.notes: New-customer prediction requires separation by customer. Future prediction for returning customers requires separation in time. Some deployments require both.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Selection on Development Accuracy
slides.caption: Synthetic independent chance predictions: 80 development cases per candidate.
slides.description: Expected selected development accuracy rises from 50% for one candidate to 56.49%, 60.40%, and 63.93% for five, twenty, and one hundred candidates. Expected fresh accuracy stays at 50%.
slides.notes: Each candidate has true accuracy one-half under the imposed independent Bernoulli model. The maximum development score increases with the number compared. Fresh test correctness is independent of selection. The program verifies the analytic expectation and simulates 2,000 repetitions with 200 test cases. Real prompt candidates can be correlated, so the magnitude is illustrative.
slides.source: Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes, M7 §7.20.

slides.title: The Forecast Origin
bullets: Features end before the decision time.
The outcome window begins after the decision.
Training labels must already be observable at fitting time.
slides.notes: A database extract can contain information that did not exist at the historical prediction origin. Store measurement windows or feature timestamps to make the information constraint verifiable.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Baselines and Model Families
bullets: Compare with a constant probability or recent-history forecast.
Logistic regression supplies a probability baseline.
Trees represent conditional splits. Ensembles combine trees.
slides.notes: A complex model earns its place through performance on the intended held-out observations and decision costs. Training fit alone rewards flexibility.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Logistic Prediction
slides.intro: Transform a linear index into a binary-outcome probability.
slides.interpretation: A coefficient changes log odds. Its probability effect depends on the starting point.
slides.notes: The same index change has a larger probability effect near the middle than near zero or one. Calibration should be evaluated on the deployment population.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.3, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Preprocessing Belongs in Training
bullets: Fit imputation, scaling, and vocabulary on training records.
Choose model settings using validation data.
Keep the final test sample separate from model selection.
slides.notes: Repeatedly choosing features from test performance turns that sample into validation data. A pipeline helps preserve the training-only boundary within cross-validation.

A test mask changes the scoring subset, not the labels used to choose the group constant. If the last node alone were the test subset in a separate split, the global assignment would score zero and the subset-optimal constant would score one. Masked global scores therefore need not be subset-specific ceilings. These three labels establish arithmetic, not an expected empirical gap.

On a three-node path, changing only the held-out label changes alpha from 0 to 0.5.
Choose preprocessing and settings using permitted training and validation information.
Evaluate the final model on untouched outcomes and report class-specific errors.

bullets: A retailer combines product-support and subscription examples.
Contrasting examples can change which feature explains a response.
Evaluate the combined assistant in each consequential service context.

The selected control curves remain at zero. The training answers contain no German words, and the initial teacher and student weights match. slides.title: Contrasting Examples Change Attribution
slides.caption: Synthetic score contributions; sum loss, penalties a = 50 and c = 1,500.
slides.description: Left: with 5,000 Source A examples fixed, matched Source B examples reduce the task contribution and increase the tag contribution. Unrelated examples leave the tag contribution unchanged. Right: with 30,000 total examples, the tag contribution peaks inside the range when task similarity q is positive. Both vertical axes use score units from zero to one.
slides.notes: Source A has both a task feature and a source tag, with response-style score one. Source B has the task feature without the tag, with score zero. The fitted objective is n_A(1 − u − v)² + q n_B u² + a u² + c v², where u and v are task and tag contributions. At n_A = 5,000 and n_B = 0, the task contribution is 0.9585 and the tag contribution is 0.03195. With 100,000 matched examples, the tag contribution is 0.7605. Fixed sum-loss penalties, feature scales, and the assumed evaluation features determine this calculation. It is neither a neural-network fit nor a response probability. The full programs also vary feature scales and penalties. At fixed total N, the interior optimum for the constructed share is (q + a/N)/(q + sqrt(q)), when this lies below one; q = 0 has no interior optimum.
slides.source: M7 §§7.33–7.35. ../03_Data_and_Code/Training_Data_Mixtures/README.md https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10110v1

slides.caption: Published Qwen results: 30,000 examples, 30% constructed, 50 responses per run and epoch.

slides.title: The Same Average Can Conceal Regressions
slides.caption: Synthetic paired roster: all 1,000 attempted requests remain in the denominator.
slides.description: Both versions correctly resolve 95% of all requests. Product support improves from 95% to 98%, while refunds fall from 95% to 75% and cancellation falls from 95% to 40%. Counts are 900, 80, and 20 requests, respectively.
slides.notes: The outcomes are imposed independently of the ridge calculation. The same request IDs appear under both versions. Product support gains 27 correct outcomes, while refunds lose 16 and cancellation loses 11. These 27 recoveries and 27 regressions leave the aggregate unchanged. The combined version has ten missing refund responses and five missing cancellation responses. Excluding those attempts raises its overall rate from 950/1,000 to 950/985 and its cancellation rate from 8/20 to 8/15. The complete roster identifies that denominator change. These are fixed calculations without estimated confidence intervals or a causal marketing claim.

slides.title: Evidence for Customer Choice
bullets: Define success as completing the customer’s legitimate request.
Report cancellations, refunds, escalation, and unanswered requests.
Choose checkpoints on development requests; evaluate on fresh requests.
Review both positive and negative machine judgments against a stated rubric.
slides.notes: A high average service score does not establish that customers can exercise a consequential option. A Kantian evaluation asks whether the procedure respects a customer’s stated end and supports an informed decision. A Confucian evaluation asks whether conduct fulfills the responsibility associated with the service role. Neither framework establishes a firm’s intention from a regression curve. In the paper’s bird-persona check, humans accepted 55.5% of 220 machine-positive responses as coherent personas. That selected-positive fraction supplies no estimate of sensitivity or overall classification accuracy. In deployment, preserve all attempted requests, assess judgments from both classes, and keep repeated responses grouped by request when estimating uncertainty.
slides.source: M7 §§7.33–7.35. ../03_Data_and_Code/Training_Data_Mixtures/README.md https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10110v1 M9 §9.18.3. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md

bullets: Precision: what fraction of reviewed cases are positive?
Recall: what fraction of positives enter the queue?
Calibration: do predicted probabilities match observed frequencies?
slides.notes: The appropriate contact fraction should match staff capacity. A ranking measure and a probability measure answer different questions. Neither by itself measures the causal effect of contacting a customer.

slides.caption: A synthetic transformation squares initially calibrated probabilities.
slides.description: Squaring the scores preserves their order but changes the probability scale. Ranking performance can remain unchanged while expected counts become wrong.
slides.notes: For q=p squared, the original outcome frequency p equals the square root of q. Expected contribution calculations need probabilities with the relevant interpretation.

slides.title: Identical Ranking, Different Probabilities
slides.caption: Synthetic customers and imposed scores: both models have AUC 0.803. Each plotted group contains 20 customers.
slides.description: Model A probabilities match group purchase shares on the diagonal. Model B retains the same order and ties but stretches low and high probabilities. Common axes run from zero to one.
slides.notes: The same 80 eligible customers have 36 purchases and 44 nonpurchases in one next-month window. Each can purchase at most once. Group calibration of Model A is imposed; no trained model or future performance claim is involved. No uncertainty interval is attached to this fixed constructed population.
slides.source: M7 Section 7.23. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: AUC Alone Does Not Set Inventory
slides.caption: Same 80 synthetic customers. Smaller Brier scores indicate less squared probability error.
slides.notes: AUC gives half credit to tied positive-negative pairs: 1272/1584 = 53/66 for both models. A strictly increasing score transformation preserves ordering. The sum of probabilities changes, making probability accuracy relevant to inventory. The Brier score is an overall probability loss, not solely a calibration measure. Purchase propensity does not identify a coupon effect.

slides.title: Token Verification and Customer Resolution
slides.caption: The target verifies decoding. Customer service requires an external criterion.
slides.description: A drafter proposes tokens, the target verifies a prefix and continues generation, and task evaluation checks the completed answer and required action. Unresolved requests go to revision or human review.
slides.notes: Use minutes 60–70 for this four-slide comparison. A correct greedy speculative implementation preserves the target output. Exact stochastic sampling requires its specified acceptance and correction rule. Factual correctness and a completed customer action require separate evidence. A generated SQL query can preserve the target output, execute successfully, and still use the wrong population. Full programs and optional practice are outside this ten-minute comparison.

slides.title: More Progress Can Take More Time
slides.caption: Synthetic development workload. Total throughput includes prefill and EOS.
slides.description: For compatibility 0.85, block efficiency rises from 3.60 at k = 4 to 5.65 at k = 12. Throughput falls from 349.74 to 171.59 tokens per second. Ordinary generation gives 212.69.

Drafting costs 0.25q and verification 4 + 0.08q + 0.16q squared milliseconds. Values are imposed calculations, not measured device latency. Development selection chooses length three, with 365.66 tokens per second on separate evaluation requests. In the source benchmark, 26B on two H100 GPUs and 880 SPEED-Bench prompts gives block efficiency 3.27 and 4.39 at lengths four and twelve, while throughput falls from 334.0 to 209.5. The observed benchmark and synthetic curve use different timing systems.

slides.caption: SciQA: 500 test examples. Accuracy uses supplied reference prefixes.

Next-token accuracy conditions on the supplied reference prefix. Whole-answer correctness requires a separate evaluation. Re-evaluate dependent components when the target changes. Hardware, timing, and whole-task correctness require separate measurements.
slides.source: Galgani and coauthors (2026), Table 4. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25813v1

slides.title: Failed Requests Change the Comparison
slides.caption: Twelve synthetic requests per target. Two specialized-target timeouts. Costs in dollars.
slides.notes: These are different hypothetical targets with independently constructed teacher-forced and free-response observations. Word tokens use whitespace splitting. Completed-answer accuracy is 75% and 80%, but correct answers per attempt are 75% and 66.67%. Each target also has one correct answer with an incomplete action. Compute costs 0.002 dollars per second and unresolved requests incur 0.20 dollars for triage. Total costs are 0.848 and 1.024 dollars. Later human resolution and review delay are unobserved. Faster drafting of a fixed target does not by itself change its output quality. Evaluate the actual policy, action, referral work, and access to review.
slides.source: M7 §§7.31–7.32. ../03_Data_and_Code/Inference_Efficiency/README.md

slides.title: Calibrate a Demand Interval
slides.intro: Freeze the predictor. Score 99 reserved stores with absolute errors.
slides.interpretation: Exchangeable calibration and new scores give at least 90% marginal coverage.
slides.notes: The fitted predictor and score are chosen using training data alone. The coverage probability averages over the calibration sample and a new observation, conditional on training. It does not guarantee 90% coverage within every customer group or after a demand shift. With eight calibration cases the required ninth rank gives an infinite threshold. Prediction intervals concern future outcomes; confidence intervals for mean demand concern a population quantity.
slides.source: M7 §7.24. ../03_Data_and_Code/Conformal_Prediction/README.md

slides.title: Aggregate Coverage Can Hide Segment Errors
slides.caption: Same 100 synthetic stores. Mean width: 20.0 pooled; 20.8 within segment.
slides.description: Pooled intervals cover 90 of 100 stores: 80 of 80 regular and 10 of 20 volatile stores. Separate calibration covers 98 overall: 80 regular and 18 volatile. The common axis runs from zero to one hundred percent and a dashed line marks the ninety-percent target.
slides.notes: Calibration uses 80 regular and 19 volatile stores distinct from evaluation. The pooled threshold is ten demand units. Separate predefined-group thresholds are eight and twenty, producing widths of sixteen and forty. Their weighted mean is 20.8. These are constructed records and an imposed predictor. Within-group guarantees require exchangeability within groups and sufficient calibration data; statistical coverage alone does not establish customer benefit.
slides.source: M7 §7.24.2. ../03_Data_and_Code/Conformal_Prediction/demand_intervals.py

slides.title: A Complaint Can Have Several Plausible Labels
slides.caption: Synthetic probabilities; 19 labeled calibration cases; three unlabeled queries.
slides.description: At probability threshold 0.35, the three queries yield billing alone, billing plus delivery, and an empty set. Multiple-label and empty sets go to human review. The singleton is a routing candidate.
slides.notes: The eighteenth ordered true-class score is 0.65. Include a label when one minus its probability is at most 0.65. The queries have no observed labels, so the example reports no test accuracy. Marginal set coverage does not control error conditional on singleton routing. Evaluate referral error, queue size, waiting time, and customer consequences separately. An empty set is a reason to seek information; it is not proof of distribution change.

slides.title: Reconstruction and Customer Review
slides.caption: A preserves dominant variation while losing the signal required for review.
slides.description: Four invented vectors have style coordinates of plus or minus 100 and review coordinates of plus or minus 1. A has 0.010% total FVU and 0 of 2 review recall; B has 0.040% FVU and 2 of 2 recall. Rescaling style to 1 reverses the FVU ranking without changing routing.
slides.notes: The four equally weighted cases are synthetic; no model was trained. A keeps style and sets review to zero. B multiplies style by 0.98 and preserves review. The rule sends cases for review when the reconstructed second coordinate is positive. Accuracy over all four cases is 50% and 100%, while recall uses the two positive cases. Both comparisons use identical records.
slides.source: M7 §§7.39–7.40. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Aggregate Error Weights the Components
slides.intro: At fixed coordinate units and a common evaluation population:
slides.interpretation: Component variation sets the weights. Decision importance requires separate evaluation.
slides.notes: V_j is the sum of squared deviations from the coordinate mean. Each component FVU divides its reconstruction error by positive V_j. The identity uses orthogonal coordinates and the same population. Delisle and Tan study a dominant activation direction in sparse autoencoders. Their bypass retains the projection in the final reconstruction; this is not evidence that deleting the first customer-data component improves a marketing decision.
slides.source: M7 §§7.39–7.40. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md Nathan Delisle and Chenhao Tan, Massive Activations Confound Sparse Autoencoders, v1. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13548v1

slides.title: Exact Reconstruction, Different Features
slides.caption: The selected dictionary determines the contribution removed.
slides.description: Contributions (1,1) and (1,-1), or (1,2) and (1,-2), both sum to (2,0). Dashed arrows translate the second contribution. Removing the first leaves squared error 2 or 5. Positive coefficients multiply unit vectors; the coefficient penalties differ.
slides.notes: Set the two slopes to one and two. The positive coefficient sums are two times square root of 2 and two times square root of 5, so equal reconstruction can coexist with different full sparse-autoencoder losses. Removing a contribution measures its role within the chosen dictionary; a psychological interpretation requires evidence connecting it to customer behavior.
slides.source: M7 §§7.39–7.40. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Evaluate a Feature Before Naming It
bullets: Compare matched features across repeated fits.
Evaluate retained information on the intended task.
Check the proposed meaning against independent records.
Keep causal claims and permission evidence separate.
slides.notes: Feature ordering and any relevant sign convention require an explicit matching procedure. Reproducibility, task utility, and substantive meaning answer different questions. Feature intervention assesses the changed model; an economic causal interpretation needs additional assumptions and evidence. Full calculations and AI-assisted coding extensions are available as optional ungraded practice.

slides.intro: Suppose false positives cost $C_{FP}$ and false negatives cost $C_{FN}$.
slides.interpretation: With costs 1 and 9, the threshold is 0.10 under this simplified classification loss.
slides.notes: Correct classifications have zero cost in this example. Capacity constraints and different action effects require a richer decision model.

slides.title: Coupon Targeting Includes the Untreated Outcome
slides.caption: Synthetic probabilities and costs. High treated response can have negative incremental value.
slides.description: Customer A has treated purchase probability 0.80 and contribution -5.20 dollars. B has probability 0.30 and contribution 2.50 dollars under the stated coupon model.
slides.notes: Contribution is 40 dollars, discount 5 dollars per treated purchase, and contact cost 2 dollars. Baseline probabilities are 0.78 and 0.15. Discount expense applies to purchases that would also have occurred without the coupon.

slides.title: Queue Metrics
slides.intro: Compute metrics from the synthetic confusion matrix.

tp, fn, fp, tn = 30, 20, 70, 880
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)
accuracy = (tp + tn) / (tp + fn + fp + tn)

slides.title: McBroken Forecasting
bullets: Predict availability on a later date.
Retain a separate count of unknown future labels.
Compare baseline and fitted forecasts on the same observed outcomes.
slides.notes: An unknown future status is not an observed available restaurant. Dropping missing labels changes the evaluated population and can make an apparently strong forecast depend on observation coverage.

slides.title: Prediction and Outcome Coverage
slides.caption: McBroken forecasts use later dates and observed-label denominators.
slides.description: The figure compares forecast performance while preserving the distinction between known labels and missing future outcomes.
slides.notes: The course example checks information availability at the forecast origin and uses chronological evaluation. Missing outcome counts remain alongside accuracy measures.

slides.title: Three Alerts, Different Decisions
slides.caption: Three synthetic stores; one twenty-minute event of each type.
slides.notes: Training has 2,160 store-minutes, validation has 1,080 normal store-minutes, and evaluation has 1,080 later store-minutes. Six whole evaluation runs remain nominal. The event label includes the successful campaign. An alert identifies unusualness under the fitted reference; a response requires interpretation and supporting evidence. slides.title: A Strong Symptom Can Follow the Cause
slides.caption: Synthetic payment event: support contacts rank first by mean standardized deviation.
slides.description: The imposed service interruption directly changes latency and completion and produces support contacts with a five-minute lag. Support persists after recovery; its average deviation in the true window is 30.45.
slides.notes: The cause is imposed by the data generator. The score only uses observed variables. Within the true interval the mean standardized support deviation is 30.4533. Within the matched alert interval it is 32.5105. Both are descriptive rankings. A real repair decision needs payment traces or other evidence that supports the proposed mechanism. All score scales and floors are defined in M7 §7.29.2.

slides.title: Evaluate Minutes and Monitoring Runs
slides.caption: Same 1,080 test minutes; six wholly nominal runs; constructed events include a campaign.
slides.notes: Mean and maximum standardized deviations use the same six features and training-only store/phase references. Thresholds are the 1,070th ordered validation score: approximately 0.774785 and 1.686227. Alerts strictly exceed the threshold. There are nine and seven alert minutes outside labeled windows. Five follow payment recovery while support contacts remain high. These are fixed-panel results, not population performance estimates. Staff effort depends on the grouping of alert minutes into review requests.

slides.title: Any Overlap Can Reward a Broad Prediction
slides.caption: Same true event [40,60); interval endpoints are exclusive.
slides.description: Precise [40,60), delayed [45,65), and full-window [0,120) predictions all overlap. Their intersection-over-union values are 1.00, 0.60, and one-sixth.
slides.notes: The delayed prediction intersects fifteen true minutes and spans a twenty-five-minute union. Absolute onset errors are zero, five, and forty minutes. The actual synthetic payment alert interval is [40,65), whose IoU is 20/25=0.80 because support contacts persist. Missed events and multiple-event matching require explicit conventions; the program permits one event per run.

slides.title: An Earlier Value Must Respect Its Information Set
slides.intro: Two possible futures follow the same two missing measurements.
slides.code:
from timing_and_missingness import causal_fill

a = causal_fill([None, None, 90, 92], 100)
b = causal_fill([None, None, 900, 92], 100)
assert a[:2] == b[:2] == [100, 100]
slides.check: Run from Anomaly_Diagnosis. The training median is fixed at 100.
slides.notes: Forward filling followed by backward filling would set the two earlier values to 90 or 900. This displayed alternative uses a training median before any observation and carries forward only past values thereafter. The retail program imputes the training-group median directly and retains missingness. Dropping missing rows also changes positions: observed minutes two and three become rows zero and one if timestamps are discarded.

slides.title: Require Evidence for the Diagnosis
bullets: Provide measurements, units, missingness, and predicted intervals.
Separate observed changes, causal hypotheses, and the next check.
Evaluate factual support and proposed action on the full run roster.
slides.notes: Nine evidence packets include all test runs and no true cause or event boundary. Supply the separate variable dictionary, not the generator or incident table. Public labels provide practice answers; new incidents are needed for independent evaluation after revision. No LLM calls were made for these saved results. Keep invalid, missing, and abstained responses visible. An unusual mHealth logging pattern alone does not establish health, intent, or misconduct.
slides.source: M7 §§7.29–7.30. ../03_Data_and_Code/Anomaly_Diagnosis/README.md

slides.title: Accuracy and Failure Costs
slides.caption: Constructed cases: pooled accuracy rises from 78% to 86%.
slides.description: Routine accuracy rises from 75% to 90% on eighty cases; consequential accuracy falls from 90% to 70% on twenty.
slides.notes: Fourteen paired cases improve and six regress. Stipulated failure costs of one dollar for routine tasks and twenty dollars for consequential tasks give losses of sixty and 128 dollars. The additional four consequential failures outweigh the twelve avoided routine failures. These are constructed values, not measured model performance.

slides.title: Paired Regression Checks
slides.intro: The same one hundred constructed cases are scored under both configurations.
slides.code:
improved, regressed, cases = 14, 6, 100
gain_pp = 100 * (improved - regressed) / cases
old_loss = 20 * 1 + 2 * 20
new_loss = 8 * 1 + 6 * 20
print(gain_pp, old_loss, new_loss)

The challenger improves this loss only below a ratio of three. Inference fees, setup costs, and other outcomes require additional terms.

slides.title: Equal Grader Scores, Different Consequences
slides.caption: Twelve synthetic statements; all cases remain in the scoring denominators.
slides.description: Both graders have 81.25 percent balanced accuracy. The permissive grader has one false approval and one false rejection, with imposed loss eleven. The cautious grader has two false rejections and one referral, with imposed loss two and one-half.
slides.notes: There are eight reference PASS statements and four reference FAIL statements. The permissive grader correctly accepts seven and rejects three. The cautious grader correctly accepts five and rejects all four; it abstains on one reference PASS. Valid-decision coverage is twelve of twelve and eleven of twelve. False approval costs ten loss units, false rejection one, and perfect human resolution after referral one-half. A cost change can reverse the ranking. These are constructed decisions, not measured model performance.

slides.title: Reference Judgments and Customer Interests
bullets: Give every reference judgment a reason.
Keep missing, invalid, and abstained outputs visible.
Reserve new cases from rubric and prompt revision.
Assess whose consequences the scoring rule includes.
slides.notes: The public practice labels are disclosed. To estimate generalization, collect new statements and independent judgments, resolve or report disagreements, freeze the rubric, and evaluate on cases not used for revision. Reference agreement does not establish ethical validity. Use five minutes for the grader comparison and five for forecast interpretation after the twenty-minute anomaly case. The conformal prediction exercise remains in the Python block.

slides.title: A Correct Total Can Misassign Activity
slides.caption: Synthetic users. The same aggregate selects a different person for review.

slides.notes: The customer decision depends on which user receives each value. Matching the overall mean therefore leaves a consequential error undetected. The course grader compares every roster user and denominator. Independent tests include this counterexample, missing users, duplicate keys, invalid dates, and nonfinite outputs. An independently written SQL query checks the actual mHealth task results.

slides.title: Outputs, Actions, and the Checker
bullets: Output: complete and accurate customer counts.
Actions: permitted files, commands, revisions, and resource use.
Checker: detection of decision-relevant errors.
slides.notes: These judgments can disagree. An accurate table may follow an unauthorized input change. A weak checker may accept an invalid table. Record observable tool actions and state changes; a generated explanation does not reveal the model’s internal reasoning. The provided CSV checker executes no candidate code and supplies no execution sandbox.

Keep August answers outside the model workspace.
Evaluate the frozen program on August.
Report validity, failures, analyst effort, and total cost.

Fresh conversations reduce carryover, and five repeated runs per configuration describe variability on this task. Full AI comparisons are optional ungraded practice; the released numerical results are local reference calculations and separately labeled hypothetical costs.

slides.title: An Omitted Feature Bias
bullets: The allocation assumes that auxiliary feature bias equals zero.
Adding an omitted coefficient of 0.3 changes the expected feature estimate from 0.4 to 0.657143.
Total coefficient MSE rises from 0.009921 to 0.076043.
slides.notes: These are analytic moments in the invented four-profile design. Both source variances equal one, with 216 primary and 1,296 auxiliary responses. The fitted model retains intercept and price bias; the sensitivity adds a feature bias to the auxiliary mean. Expected feature-coefficient error equals 0.3 times 1296/1512. The 0.01 MSE target fails because of the omitted bias restriction.
slides.source: Jasin, Lin, and Zhang (2026), Bias Geometry and the Value of Auxiliary Data. https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7734298

slides.title: Sampling Variance and Persistent Bias
slides.caption: Invented example. Both source counts grow in fixed proportion; the omitted feature bias stays at 0.3.
slides.description: The navy curve gives correct-model MSE, declining from 0.009921 toward zero as sample size multiplies by up to 32. The orange curve includes omitted feature bias and approaches a gray squared-bias floor of 0.066122. A dotted line marks the original 0.01 target. Source ratios, variances, and true coefficients remain fixed.
slides.notes: At 32 times the initial counts, correct-model MSE is 0.000310 and omitted-bias MSE is 0.066432. A larger sample narrows sampling variation while preserving the expected coefficient error. Adding the feature to the fitted bias dictionary restores correct specification but makes all three primary features confounded with unrestricted auxiliary bias. At the original 216 primary observations, the corrected model has MSE 3/216 = 0.013889.
slides.source: Jasin, Lin, and Zhang (2026), Bias Geometry and the Value of Auxiliary Data. https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7734298

slides.title: Human Validation of the Bias Model
bullets: A bias feature excluded by a significance cutoff may still matter for the decision.
Reserve human respondents and concepts from model and feature selection.
Repeated ratings require a dependence model before they count as independent information.
slides.notes: In the paper Table 1 Panel B, the Republican-indicator bias has p = 0.034 and is excluded by the 0.01 threshold. Holding the five primary features fixed and adding that bias feature makes the bias dictionary cover the full primary feature space, yielding zero auxiliary value under the expanded worst-case model. This is a sensitivity implication, not an empirical re-estimation. The reported 74 and 32 percent savings come from retrospective calibrations assuming auxiliary cost is one percent of primary cost. M7 Section 7.37 provides full Python and interpretation.
slides.source: Jasin, Lin, and Zhang (2026), Bias Geometry and the Value of Auxiliary Data. https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7734298

slides.title: Coding Exercise: A Forecast Evaluation
bullets: Verify a calibration rank on a hand-checkable sample.
Compare segment coverage and interval widths on the same stores.
Explain why singleton-routing error needs a separate evaluation.
slides.notes: Run demand_intervals.py, complaint_sets.py, and the six tests in Conformal_Prediction. The fixed synthetic records require no fitted model. Additional practice uses the existing repeated-selection and paired-upgrade examples. Full programs appear in M7 §§7.24–7.25.
slides.source: M7 §§7.24–7.25. ../03_Data_and_Code/Conformal_Prediction/README.md

slides.title: Targeting and Delivered Opportunities
bullets: An apparently neutral target can produce unequal delivery.
Evaluate exposure and error costs across relevant groups.
Housing, credit, and employment applications require their specific legal context.
slides.notes: The DOJ's Meta housing-ad settlement addresses discriminatory delivery as well as targeting tools. That case is evidence about housing advertising and should not be generalized into a single rule for all products.
slides.source: DOJ, United States v. Meta Platforms. https://www.justice.gov/crt/case/united-states-v-meta-platforms-inc-fka-facebook-inc-sdny

slides.title: Prediction Discussion
bullets: Which error uses scarce review capacity?
Which feature becomes available too late?
Does the score support a forecast, an intervention, or both?
slides.notes: A deployment decision needs an explicit chain from information to prediction to action. Each link has its own empirical requirements.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.9, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

title: Recommendation Systems and Customer Goals
objectives: Define candidate generation, scoring, and ranking.
Evaluate top-k recommendations on an appropriate history and denominator.
Compare relevance, novelty, customer goals, and explanation accuracy.

slides.title: A Returning-Customer Decision
bullets: An mHealth user returns to log a meal.
The system chooses among eligible categories using earlier histories.
The objective may include familiar relevance and a stated variety goal.
slides.notes: The next logged basket differs from the next item row. A basket can contain several relevant categories. Availability and the customer's goal constrain which recommendations are useful.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.15, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: The Candidate Set
bullets: Candidate generation determines what can be recommended.
Scoring compares eligible items using current information.
Ranking chooses order and applies list constraints.
slides.notes: A strong ranking model cannot recover an item excluded during candidate generation. Evaluation must retain the candidate-set definition as well as the ranked output.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.10, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Recommendation Models
bullets: Content models compare item attributes and customer histories.
Collaborative models learn patterns across customers and items.
Popularity and personal-frequency rules provide useful baselines.
slides.notes: A content model can help with new items that lack interactions. A collaborative model benefits from shared behavior but faces cold-start and selected-exposure problems.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.10, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Histories Must Precede the Basket
slides.caption: mHealth evaluation freezes histories and candidate sets at the forecast origin.
slides.description: Training histories precede validation and test baskets. Later outcomes do not define candidate eligibility or tune the final model.
slides.notes: Returning-user prediction uses each user's earlier history while holding out later baskets. Holding out complete users instead evaluates performance for new users.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.15.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Recall Among Relevant Categories
slides.intro: Let $L_i$ be the top-k list and $B_i$ the categories in the next observed basket.
slides.interpretation: The denominator is the number of relevant basket categories for that user-event.
slides.notes: Report how empty baskets and unavailable categories are handled. Average per event or per user according to the target population, and retain the chosen weighting rule.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Position Matters
slides.intro: Discount lower-ranked relevant items when their positions affect exposure.
slides.interpretation: NDCG divides by the best attainable DCG for the same relevance labels.
slides.notes: NDCG depends on the candidate set and relevance definition. Unobserved engagement is not necessarily a negative preference label because exposure is selective.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Basket Associations
bullets: Support counts how often items occur together.
Confidence conditions on the antecedent item.
Lift compares confidence with the consequent's marginal prevalence.
slides.notes: Association rules are descriptive. A positive lift can reflect common meal occasions or other causes rather than a response to recommendation. Evaluate rules on later baskets.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.17, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Lift Changes the Baseline Comparison
slides.caption: mHealth basket rules use distinct baskets and future validation.
slides.description: The chart compares rule confidence with a marginal-prevalence benchmark. Common items can have high confidence with little lift.
slides.notes: Counting item rows instead of distinct baskets changes the denominator and can inflate associations through repeated entries.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.17, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Relevance and a Customer Goal
slides.intro: Combine relevance $s_j$ with a goal score $g_j$ using an explicit weight.
slides.interpretation: The scores need a comparable scale before the weight has a clear interpretation.
slides.notes: A goal score should reflect a defined customer objective and validated measurement. The weight does not become a preference estimate merely because a programmer sets it.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.12.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Small Weight Changes Can Change the First Item
slides.caption: Synthetic item scores. Relevance and goal scores stay fixed.
slides.description: A ranks first at low goal weights, B in a middle range, and C at high weights. The maximizing item switches at crossings even though each score changes smoothly.
slides.notes: A recommendation can be discontinuous in a tuning weight. Sensitivity analysis should report the ranking itself, not only smooth average scores.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.12.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: A Three-Item Basket Check
slides.intro: The list contains A, B, and C. The basket contains A and C.
slides.code:
from math import log2
ranked = ['A', 'B', 'C']
relevant = {'A', 'C'}
recall = len(set(ranked) & relevant) / len(relevant)
dcg = sum((x in relevant) / log2(r+2)
          for r,x in enumerate(ranked))
ideal = 1 + 1/log2(3)
assert recall == 1.0
slides.check: Recall is 1.0, while NDCG is about 0.920 because B occupies the second position.
slides.notes: The calculation uses binary relevance. It assumes all relevant items are eligible and that the observation window defines a valid basket.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: LLM Explanations
bullets: Explain a recommendation using verified item attributes.
Check whether stated reasons are factually supported.
Evaluate explanation effects separately from ranking quality.
slides.notes: An explanation can sound plausible while inventing a nutritional property or claiming a nonexistent personal preference. Factual support and behavioral effects require distinct evaluations.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.13, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Offline and Online Outcomes
bullets: A hit in a historical basket measures predictive overlap.
A recommendation changes exposure and may change behavior.
A randomized policy comparison measures the intervention outcome.
slides.notes: An unrecorded category can reflect absent exposure, unavailable products, or dislike. Offline metrics evaluate the resulting recorded outcomes under their measurement conditions. The effect of displaying a new list requires a causal comparison.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.15, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Personalization Can Improve Consumer Welfare
bullets: A ranking experiment found more search and purchasing.
Its structural model estimated higher consumer surplus despite profit weighting.
Separate experimental behavior from model-dependent welfare.
slides.notes: Welfare Effects of Personalized Rankings compares personalized rankings with uniform bestseller rankings. The claim here follows the verified publisher abstract; the final full text was not retrieved. Targeted Advertising as Implicit Recommendation supplies a theoretical counterpoint in which strategic targeting and endogenous prices alter welfare. Neither study establishes that all personalization helps or harms consumers. See M7 Section 7.21.
slides.source: https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.1441 and https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0117

slides.title: Coding Exercise: Ranking with a Goal
bullets: Compare popularity and personal-frequency baselines.
Tune the goal weight on validation baskets.
Evaluate the fixed choice on later baskets.
Assess one generated explanation against item attributes.
slides.notes: Run ../03_Data_and_Code/Lecture_Examples/session_examples.py S12 for the NDCG check. The full mHealth m07.py program defines the candidate and basket windows. Preserve the final test period for evaluation.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Customer Control of Recommendations
bullets: A customer can accept a suggested goal or reject it.
Factual explanations should distinguish evidence from an inferred preference.
Evaluate whether the interface respects a revised goal.
slides.notes: A nominal control that does not affect the recommendation can leave the customer unable to change the policy. A recommendation evaluation should record both the chosen setting and its implemented effect.
slides.source: ETHICS_AND_REGULATION.md, M7.

slides.title: Recommendation Discussion
bullets: Which relevant item was excluded before scoring?
Whose goal determines the ranking weight?
What evidence would show improved customer experience?
slides.notes: The full policy includes eligibility, ranking, explanation, and updates after use. A useful evaluation identifies which component changed.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.12, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

practice: Compare ranking baselines, calculate NDCG, and assess a goal-weight sensitivity.
application: Check a generated recommendation explanation and design an online outcome comparison.

title: Adaptive Recommendations and Marketing Budgets
objectives: Trace how recommendations affect future training data.
Evaluate list objectives and customer goals.
Allocate a fixed marketing budget using marginal response.
Assess forecast coverage after demand changes and respect delayed outcome information.
Distinguish estimated response uncertainty from the choice and justification of an objective.

slides.title: Recommendations Shape the Paths Customers Follow
slides.description: A gardener consults a tablet beside familiar and exploratory paths through different fruit trees. The paths represent selected exposure and future opportunities.
slides.notes: A frequently used path produces more observations from its existing destinations. Exploration changes which preferences can be learned.
slides.source: Original conceptual illustration. 05_Slides/assets/PROVENANCE.md.

slides.title: An Adaptive Policy
bullets: A model selects exposure using existing interaction histories.
Customers respond to the displayed options.
Retraining incorporates those selected responses.
slides.notes: The policy changes the environment that supplies future training data. The update rule and retraining schedule belong in the definition of the intervention.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Selected Exposure Creates a Feedback Loop
slides.caption: Recommendation choices change exposure and the observations available for subsequent model training.
slides.description: Recommendations affect exposure, exposure affects observed responses, and those responses inform subsequent training and recommendations.
slides.notes: A popularity loop can concentrate observation among already visible items. Randomized exploration or additional evaluation data can change what the system learns.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: The Evaluation Horizon Includes Learning
slides.caption: A temporary intervention can persist through subsequent model updates.
slides.description: The intervention changes responses during the campaign. A retrained model can preserve information from those responses after the campaign ends.
slides.notes: Freezing the model blocks the retraining channel but can leave direct changes in customer behavior. These policies require separate definitions and, where feasible, separate comparisons.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.1.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Demand Changes Can Break Earlier Coverage
slides.caption: Same synthetic stores; forecasts and calibration remain fixed.
slides.notes: Demand rises by twenty-five units at every evaluation store. Pooled width remains twenty and average segment width remains 20.8. The calculations describe an imposed change in demand conditional on the same features. Chronological evaluation uses only outcomes observed by the forecast origin, including any label delay. A recent calibration window alone does not restore the ordinary exchangeability guarantee. Different horizons and dependent observations require methods and evaluation appropriate to those settings.
slides.source: M8 §8.21; complete Python in M7 §7.24.3. ../03_Data_and_Code/Conformal_Prediction/demand_intervals.py

slides.title: Customer Goals and Platform Objectives
bullets: Clicks reveal a response within an offered environment.
Considered preferences can differ from immediate engagement.
Measure satisfaction, unwanted repetition, and customer-stated goals.
slides.notes: A higher click count can coexist with regret or frustration. A system can combine behavior with explicit goals while recognizing that each measure has its own errors.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.2.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: A List Objective
slides.intro: A list combines item relevance with category variety.
slides.interpretation: The variety weight $\lambda$ is expressed in the same units as the relevance score.
slides.notes: A weighted sum requires a substantive choice of scales and tradeoffs. A customer replenishing a familiar basket may prefer a different weight from a customer seeking variety.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Two Three-Item Lists
slides.caption: Synthetic scores. The lists tie at a variety weight of 0.20.
slides.notes: Suppose A and B are coffee, C is tea, and D is fruit, with the relevance scores shown. Increasing category variety reduces total relevance by 0.20 under these scores.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Model-Based and Experimental Evidence
bullets: A fitted choice model can compare alternative recommenders.
A randomized perturbation can test predicted response patterns.
Engagement, retention, revenue, and welfare are distinct outcomes.
slides.notes: The Netflix study discussed in the notes uses a fitted choice model and an experimental check. Its replacement-recommender comparisons are model-based counterfactuals with specific exposure conditions.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.1.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Marketing-Mix Modeling
bullets: Weekly channel spending can have delayed effects.
Response can saturate at high exposure.
Spending decisions can respond to anticipated demand.
slides.notes: Trend, seasonality, promotions, and media can move together. A fitted media component requires an identification argument before it is interpreted as a causal contribution.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.3, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Carryover
slides.intro: A geometric accumulated-exposure measure retains earlier spending.
slides.interpretation: A 100-unit pulse with $\rho=0.5$ gives 100, 50, 25, and 12.5 in successive periods.
slides.notes: This definition is unnormalized. Under constant spending s, its long-run level is s divided by one minus rho. Coefficients must follow the implementation's normalization.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.3, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Saturation and the Next Dollar
slides.intro: A concave response has declining marginal contribution.
slides.interpretation: Budget transfers depend on marginal response at the current allocation.
slides.notes: Average response summarizes all earlier units of spending. The next small transfer depends on the local slope, with units of contribution per spending unit.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Average and Marginal Returns Can Disagree
slides.caption: Synthetic known response curves. Total spending is fixed at 60 thousand dollars.
slides.description: At the starting allocation, A has higher average return while B has higher marginal return. A transfer from A to B increases total contribution.
slides.notes: The response curves are 100 times one minus exp(-sA/20) and 80 times one minus exp(-sB/40). The interior allocation equalizes marginal returns.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: The Fixed-Budget Optimum
slides.intro: Solve equal marginal returns for the imposed curves.
slides.code:
from math import exp, log
budget = 60
a = (log(2.5) + budget/40) / (1/20 + 1/40)
b = budget - a
ma = 5 * exp(-a/20)
mb = 2 * exp(-b/40)
assert abs(ma-mb) < 1e-12
slides.check: The allocation is about 32.22 to A and 27.78 to B, in thousands of dollars.
slides.notes: The closed-form result applies to these known concave curves and an interior fixed-budget optimum. Different constraints or uncertain response functions require a revised calculation.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: The Objective Changes the Chosen Discount
slides.caption: Known synthetic functions; 0.1-point search grid. The 3% complaint cap is an imposed exercise condition.
slides.notes: The list price is USD 20 and unit cost is USD 4. Known mean profit is 10+0.4a-0.01a squared; expected quantity is profit divided by the unit margin. Revenue is price times quantity. The assumed complaint probability is 0.01+0.0001a squared. All quantities are per eligible customer over the promotion week. The cap is hypothetical and carries no legal or ethical authority. It reduces profit by approximately USD 0.348 relative to the unconstrained profit maximum.
slides.source: ../03_Data_and_Code/Dose_Response/decision_objectives.py; ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Estimated Responses and Customer Judgment
bullets: A search over estimated curves also selects estimation noise.
A proposed intensity needs support and independent policy evaluation.
Complaint rates leave consent, truthful communication, and refusal to be assessed.
slides.notes: The preceding table optimizes known functions. Estimated curves introduce sampling and modeling uncertainty, especially near boundaries and in poorly represented groups. Customer agency requires reasons for the practice and safeguards that remain binding when profit falls. M9 Section 9.18.1 connects this distinction to Kantian respect and Confucian trustworthiness. The observational mHealth logs do not establish effects of assigned notification intensity.
slides.source: ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md; ../03_Data_and_Code/Dose_Response/README.md; ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Restoration Changes Who Can Reach Service
slides.caption: Synthetic inputs. Bounds describe the unknown store status; population denominator: 800.
slides.description: Restoring A raises the access bounds from 68.75–87.50 percent to 81.25–100 percent. Restoring D leaves both bounds unchanged. Known and possible access use distinct markers on a common scale.
slides.notes: Both restorations lower the unavailable share among four known-status stores from one-half to one-quarter. A provides an option within five minutes to 100 people at W0. E2 already reaches C in two minutes, so D adds no people under the threshold. It still shortens travel for some origins. The bounds reflect unknown U, conditional on imposed graph times and population weights.
slides.source: Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. M8 §8.23 and M9 §9.18.2. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Profit and Access Can Rank Actions Differently
slides.caption: Equal restoration costs; imposed gains and five-minute access threshold.
slides.notes: Profit gains are hypothetical inputs, not estimated sales effects. Profit selects D; expansion of threshold-defined access selects A. A travel-time-savings objective can capture benefits of D that this threshold omits. Examine customer purposes, feasible alternatives, affordability, and the firm’s service commitments when justifying an objective. A Kantian assessment concerns the action’s maxim and respect for persons; a Confucian assessment can examine reliability and role obligations. Neither supplies a universal five-minute service standard.
slides.source: Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. M8 §8.23 and M9 §9.18.2. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Coding Exercise: A Policy Objective
bullets: Enumerate three-item lists at several variety weights.
Solve and independently grid-check the fixed-budget allocation.
Report the assumptions that change the preferred action.
slides.notes: Run ../03_Data_and_Code/Lecture_Examples/session_examples.py S13. A grid check verifies the numerical optimum within its resolution. It does not establish the imposed response curves as causal estimates.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.10, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Attention and the Optimization Target
bullets: A free service can require customer time and attention.
More exposure can benefit advertisers while burdening customers.
Evaluate voluntary use and customer outcomes alongside engagement.
slides.notes: Tim Wu's Blind Spot discusses attention markets and the difficulty of analyzing exchanges without a monetary user price. A course application should measure time, control, and value rather than equate engagement with welfare.
slides.source: Tim Wu, Blind Spot: The Attention Economy and the Law (2019). https://scholarship.law.columbia.edu/faculty_scholarship/2029/

slides.title: Policy Discussion
bullets: What changes when the recommender learns during the experiment?
Which outcome measures the customer's stated goal?
How much uncertainty in response slopes would change the budget?
slides.notes: A robust decision states the learning rule, target outcome, and support for the response function. The best numerical optimizer cannot supply those definitions.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.7, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md
